title: TA9-03279
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, a citizen of Jamaica and a citizen Antigua and Barbuda ("Antigua") seeks refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS
The following is a summary of the claimant's allegations:

The claimant was born in XXXX, Jamaica on XXXX, 1974. At seven years of age, the claimant was sexually molested by a friend of the family. The claimant was threatened with death if he told anyone. As an adolescent, the claimant realized that he was more interested in males than females. The claimant was physically assaulted by many of the boys that he grew up with and was ostracized by some of his family members. In or about 1994, the claimant moved to XXXX, Jamaica. While in XXXX, the claimant was robbed at knifepoint, physically assaulted and threatened with death. In XXXX 1998, the claimant moved to Antigua. From 1999 to 2001, the claimant was involved in a homosexual relationship with XXXX, a popular XXXX XXXX. The claimant obtained his Antiguan citizenship on XXXX, 2006. On XXXX, 2006, the claimant was physically assaulted by four or five unknown young men. The claimant fled Antigua for Canada on June 30, 2007.

On XXXX, 2007, the claimant married XXXX, a Canadian citizen. On June 27, 2008, the claimant applied for permanent residence status under the spouse/common-law partner in-Canada class. XXXX withdrew her sponsorship of the claimant on December 19, 2008, reinstated her sponsorship on December 30, 2008, then withdrew her sponsorship a second time on January 5, 2009.
The claimant filed a claim for refugee protection on February 3, 2009.
The claimant fears that if he goes back to Jamaica or Antigua he will face the same beatings and threats that he received when he lived in each of those places.
I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. My reasons are as follows. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's identity has been established through identity documents filed in evidence.2 Section 96 - Convention Refugee Grounds
The determinative issue in this section 96 analysis is whether what the claimant's fears rise to the level of persecution. I find that it does not.

To be considered persecution, the mistreatment suffered or anticipated must be serious3 and a second criterion of persecution is that the harm occurs with repetition or persistence in a systematic way.4 Cumulatively, acts of discrimination may amount to persecution and particularly where there is a denial of access to a means of existence. Denial of employment or access to employment may form the basis of link to persecution in some circumstances.

I explored the nature of the discrimination faced by the claimant to determine how serious, persistent and repetitive the mistreatment is and whether it is systematic. While the claimant's treatment simply for having a different sexual preference must have been difficult to go through, it does not, even cumulatively, amount to persecution. I find that what the claimant experienced amounted to harassment, at most, but does not rise to the level of persecution. I also find that the claimant was a victim of crime and that the victimization was not associated to his sexual orientation.

The claimant testified that he was called derogatory names, beaten, robbed and threatened on many occasions in Jamaica. The claimant believes that he was targeted in Jamaica because his attackers knew he was homosexual because of his relationship with XXXX, a local homosexual man. The claimant described the most severe incident that occurred to him in Jamaica. In 1997, as he was returning home from work, six or seven unknown men called the claimant "batty boy", a pejorative sexual slur used to describe gay, bisexual and effeminate men in Jamaica. One of the men slapped the claimant in the face and demanded his money. The claimant was told that his life would be taken if he ever came around the area again.

The claimant was called names, threatened, physically assaulted and robbed while in Jamaica. His attackers used derogatory terms to address him. Some of the names his attackers called him are slang terms used to describe gay, bisexual and effeminate men in Jamaica. These names are used by individuals in Jamaica to insult a person, whether they believe the person is gay or not. I am not persuaded that the claimant's attackers in Jamaica targeted the claimant because of his sexual orientation. No persuasive evidence was presented to indicate that the claimant was being persecuted because he is a homosexual man.

The claimant testified that, in Antigua, he had a homosexual relationship with XXXX from mid-1999 to early 2001. The claimant indicated that he was the target of assaults by young males in Antigua on many occasions. The claimant believes he was targeted because it was known he was having a relationship with XXXX, a known homosexual who was a popular XXXX XXXX. When asked if anyone ever bothered XXXX, the claimant said, "no". When asked if people knew that XXXX was gay, the claimant stated, "Yes, he doesn't hide it". When asked if Antiguans used derogatory terms to address other individuals besides gay men, the claimant testified that Antiguans call others "judge boy", "chi chi man" and "batty boy". When asked how many incidents he suffered through in Antigua, the claimant indicated that there were a lot of incidents especially when he was walking on the bad side of town. The claimant described the most severe incident as being one in 2006 when he was walking home from church. He went on to say that four or five young men called him "batty boy", chased him and kicked him. When asked if his employers in Antigua knew he was gay, the claimant testified that his employers knew he was gay, but they were old guys and it did not bother them.

The claimant is merely speculating that he was targeted in Antigua due to his sexual orientation. XXXX, a homosexual man the claimant had a relationship with, had no problems in Antigua. The claimant testified that XXXX was a popular XXXX XXXX and openly gay. When asked why he thought that XXXX would have no problems in Antigua while he had many, the claimant indicated that he was easier to beat up. The claimant stated that most of the incidents occurred in the bad side of town. No persuasive evidence was presented to indicate that homosexuals are persecuted in Antigua, and I find that the claimant was a victim of crime. Furthermore, the claimant had no problems gaining employment in Antigua. The claimant was employed as a XXXX in Antigua for some nine years, the entire time he resided there. The claimant worked for two different employers in Antigua and he indicated that his employers knew he was gay and that it did not bother them.

Considered in totality, the events the claimant describes do not amount to persecution because the claimant's future existence was not threatened in any way and this harm was not systematic. Although it is argued that some laws in Antigua make some of the sexual acts homosexuals might engage in illegal, such as buggery, they are similarly illegal when performed on women. Other sexual acts are also gender neutral, such as serious indecency.5 Homosexuality is stigmatized in Antigua6 and documentary evidence is that there is discrimination against homosexuals, but there have been no reports of discrimination or violence against a person because of their sexual orientation.7 The claimant said he believed he was assaulted because his attackers knew he was gay. Although the claimant speculates as to the motives for the beating, he noted that his homosexual partner XXXX was never assaulted. Despite the claimant's one account of violence that he speculates is due to sexual orientation, it is reasonable to expect that if discrimination and harassment were so prevalent and systematic in Antigua, there would be some reports from objective and reputed sources. The fact that there is not, indicates that harassment and discrimination against homosexuals in Antigua is not as significant a problem as the claimant believes. I find that harm due to sexual orientation is not generally systematic or persistent in Antigua.

What the claimant experienced, while unfortunate, was not persecution, even when considered cumulatively. Therefore, the claimant is not a Convention refugee and the claim with respect to his fears under section 96 of the IRPA fails. The rest of the analysis of this decision will be under section 97 of the IRPA. Section 97 - Persons in Need of Protection

The determinative issue in this section 97 analysis is whether the claimant faces a personal risk that is not faced generally by others in Antigua. Section 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA specifically excludes persons who are at a risk that is faced generally by others in or from that country. The assessment of risk must be specific to the individual8 and the evidence must establish a specific, individualized risk of harm with regard to the particular claimant.9 The risk of harm faced by the claimant cannot be indiscriminate or random, and one faced generally by the population of the country.10 The risk of harm must arise from something more than an isolated incident11 or a random act.12 Where a claimant has been specifically targeted by criminal elements the personalized risk may be made out provided the claimant is not a victim of generalized violence.13 The fact that a claimant is personally at risk does not necessarily mean that the risk is not one faced generally by others in that country.14 Discrimination faced by a segment of the population does not necessarily constitute a personalized risk for all persons who belong to that segment.15 If the risk faced by the claimant is not greater than16 or different from17 that faced by the general population, the risk is excluded and the claim fails.

In this case the claimant says he fears that if he returns to Jamaica or Antigua, he may be threatened and physically assaulted. Although the claimant had been a victim of crime while in Jamaica and Antigua, they were random and infrequent acts. There is not more than a mere possibility that the claimant would become a victim of crime if he were to return to Antigua. There is documentary evidence noted above that says people in Antigua are not generally at risk of violence for their sexual orientation. There is no persuasive evidence to indicate that the claimant would have an increased risk to becoming a victim of crime in Antigua. The claimant himself indicates that the risk of being a victim of crime was related to the area in which he was victimized. If the neighbourhood was in a bad area, there would be a higher risk of being victimized by criminals. This is not connected to his sexual identity.

While crime rates in Antigua are higher now, everyone in Antigua is equally at risk. Documentary evidence indicates that authorities attribute the crime to a new trend of gun possession among island youth and an influx of criminal deportees, with links to the drug trade, from the United States and Europe and that authorities have responded to the increased levels with increased patrols, the reintroduction of roadblocks, and stiffer fines for firearms violations.18
The claimant is not personally at a risk that is any greater or different from anyone else in that country. As such the claim under section 97(1)(b) of the IRPA fails.

There was no evidence provided that would allow a finding that the claimant would be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. None of the agents of harm the claimant is at risk from were operating with the consent or acquiescence of any public official or other person acting in official capacity. Therefore, I find the claimant is not a person in need of protection and the claim under section 97 of the IRPA fails.

The claimant does not have a well-founded fear since there is not a serious possibility of persecution, and he would not be subjected personally, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, should he return to Antigua. Accordingly, the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The claim is rejected. (signed) "Pettinella" M.
